lessons.title: My Family
objectives: Name family members and their relationships
Know families can look different
prerequisites: Can talk about people at home
explanation: A family is a group of people who love and care for each other. Some families have a mother and father; some have one parent; some live with grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins all together.
In many Indian homes, grandparents live with the family — this is called a joint family. Other families are small, called nuclear families.
Every family is different, and every family is special. What matters is that family members look after each other.

lessons.title: Who Helps Us?
objectives: Name community helpers and the work they do
Show respect and thanks for all work
explanation: Community helpers are people whose work helps everyone. Doctors and nurses help us when we're sick. Teachers help us learn. Farmers grow our food.
Firefighters put out fires. Police officers help keep us safe. Sanitation workers keep our streets clean. Postal workers deliver letters and parcels. Drivers take us places.
Every job matters. A clean street is as important as a hospital! We show respect to all workers and say thank you.

lessons.title: Building a Community
objectives: Name essential services in a community
Explain why each service matters
explanation: A community is a group of people living in the same area. To live well, a community needs services: clean water, electricity, roads, schools, hospitals, markets, parks and waste collection.
Some services are provided by the government (like government schools, roads and water supply), and some by businesses or volunteers.
When everyone takes care of shared places — not littering, saving water — the whole community benefits.

A public park everyone can use.

lessons.title: On the Move
objectives: Classify transport as land, water or air
Compare old and new ways of communicating
explanation: Transport moves people and goods. Land transport includes bicycles, buses, cars, autorickshaws, bullock carts and trains. Water transport includes boats and ships. Air transport includes aeroplanes and helicopters.
Indian Railways is one of the largest railway networks in the world and carries millions of passengers every day.
Communication means sharing messages. Long ago people sent letters by post or messengers. Today we also use phones, video calls and the internet — but a handwritten letter is still special!

lessons.title: Village or City?
objectives: Compare features of village and city life
Explain how villages and cities depend on each other
explanation: Villages are smaller places, often surrounded by fields. Many people work in farming, fishing, dairy or crafts. People often know their neighbours well.
Cities are big and busy, with many buildings, shops, offices, factories, schools and hospitals. There is more traffic and more kinds of jobs.
Villages and cities need each other. Cities need food, milk and raw materials from villages; villages use goods, services and markets from cities. Many families have members in both.

story.text: Asha from Mumbai visited her cousin Raju in a village in Maharashtra for the summer. She milked a cow and swam in the river. lessons.title: Three Kinds of Work
objectives: Sort occupations into primary, secondary and tertiary sectors
Explain the dignity of all labour
explanation: Primary sector jobs take things from nature: farming, fishing, mining, forestry.
Secondary sector jobs make things: factory workers, builders, weavers, carpenters turning raw materials into products.

Tertiary (service) sector jobs provide services: teachers, doctors, shopkeepers, drivers, bankers, software engineers. All three sectors depend on each other, and all work deserves respect — Mahatma Gandhi emphasised the dignity of manual labour.

context.text: Gandhi encouraged everyone, including students and leaders, to do manual work such as spinning and cleaning, to promote the dignity of labour.

vocabulary.meaning: a job or kind of work

making goods
providing services

examples: Cotton farmer (primary) → textile mill worker (secondary) → shopkeeper selling shirts (tertiary).
A fisherman catches fish; a cook prepares it; a waiter serves it.

lessons.title: The Panchayat and the Municipality
objectives: Explain the structure and roles of local government
Describe how citizens participate
explanation: In villages, the Panchayati Raj system governs locally. The gram sabha includes all adult voters of the village; it elects the gram panchayat, led by the sarpanch. Panchayats look after local roads, water, sanitation and village development.
In towns and cities, municipal councils or corporations, led by elected councillors and a mayor, manage water supply, waste, streetlights, roads and local health services.
The 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments (1992) strengthened these bodies and reserved seats for women and for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, so more people could take part in decisions.

context.text: The 73rd (rural) and 74th (urban) Constitutional Amendment Acts were passed in 1992; they mandate at least one-third of seats for women in local bodies, and many states have increased this to 50%.

vocabulary.meaning: all adult voters of a village

examples: A gram sabha meeting deciding on a new well.

story.title: The Women Sarpanch
story.text: In a village, many people doubted that a young woman could lead. After she was elected sarpanch, she held regular gram sabha meetings, got the school toilets built and a water pipeline laid. At the next election, she was re-elected with a big majority.

lessons.title: Together We Can: Cooperatives
objectives: Explain how cooperatives and self-help groups work
Describe a successful community initiative
explanation: A cooperative is a business owned and run by its members, who share the benefits. In the 1940s, dairy farmers in Anand, Gujarat, formed a cooperative to get fair prices for their milk. It grew into Amul.
Verghese Kurien helped build the cooperative dairy system; Operation Flood (from 1970) helped India become one of the world's largest milk producers.
Self-help groups, often of women, save money together and give small loans to members to start businesses. Community action shows that ordinary people working together can bring big change.

context.text: The Kaira District Cooperative Milk Producers' Union was formed in 1946 in Anand; India has been the world's largest milk producer in recent decades according to official and FAO data.

examples: Amul is owned by millions of dairy farmers.

story.title: The Milk Revolution
story.text: In the 1940s, dairy farmers near Anand were paid unfairly by middlemen. They decided to sell their milk together through their own cooperative. Each farmer, even with just one buffalo, became an owner. Years later, their cooperative became one of India's best-known brands — and inspired the "White Revolution".

lessons.title: What Makes a Good City?
objectives: Identify features of well-planned cities
Evaluate urban challenges and solutions
explanation: Urban planners design how land is used: housing, roads, markets, parks, schools and hospitals. Chandigarh, designed by Le Corbusier in the 1950s, is an example of a planned city.
Many Indian cities grew quickly without enough planning, leading to traffic jams, crowded informal settlements (slums), pollution and pressure on water and waste systems.
Solutions include good public transport (metro systems now run in many cities), affordable housing, protected green spaces, walking and cycling paths, and involving residents in planning.

story.title: The Street That Changed
story.text: A busy market street was choked with traffic and unsafe for walking. The city tried a pedestrian zone: cars were diverted, benches and trees added. Shopkeepers worried at first — but more people walked and shopped. Within a year, sales were up and the air was cleaner.

lessons.title: Fair Access for All
objectives: Analyse unequal access to services
Evaluate policies that aim to reduce inequality
explanation: Not everyone has equal access to good schools, health care, clean water or jobs. Differences can depend on income, location (rural or urban), gender, caste, disability and other factors.

Governments use policies to reduce inequality: the Right to Education Act (2009) for free schooling for ages 6–14, public health programmes, food security schemes, and reservations in education and jobs for historically disadvantaged groups.
Evaluating policies means asking: who benefits, what are the results, what gaps remain, and how could it be improved? People reasonably debate the best approaches.

context.text: The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act came into force in 2010.
Policies like reservations are debated in Indian public life; supporters and critics offer different arguments about their design and effects.

story.title: The Long Walk to School
story.text: In a remote village, the nearest secondary school was 10 km away. Many girls stopped studying after Class 8. When a state scheme gave bicycles to girls, more continued to high school. Researchers studied the effect — and found enrolment rose. One small policy changed many futures.

lessons.title: Social Institutions
objectives: Explain major social institutions and socialisation
Analyse social change in Indian communities
explanation: Sociology studies how societies are organised. Social institutions are lasting structures that meet basic needs: family, education, religion, economy and government.
Socialisation is how we learn norms, values and roles — first from family, then school, friends, media and community.

Communities change: urbanisation, technology, education and migration have reshaped families (more nuclear families), work and gender roles in India. Sociologists such as M. N. Srinivas studied these changes, describing processes like Sanskritisation and Westernisation.

context.text: Concepts like Sanskritisation are analytical tools proposed by sociologists and debated by later scholars.

examples: Learning greetings like namaste or salaam at home — socialisation.

lessons.title: Measuring Progress
objectives: Compare measures of development
Design a participatory development project
explanation: Development is often measured by GDP (the value of goods and services produced). But GDP doesn't show whether people are healthy, educated or happy.

The Human Development Index (HDI), introduced by the UNDP with economists Mahbub ul Haq and Amartya Sen, combines life expectancy, education and income. Sen argued development means expanding people's real freedoms and capabilities.
Participatory development involves community members in deciding priorities and designing solutions, rather than imposing projects from outside. It often leads to more lasting results.

context.text: The first Human Development Report was published by UNDP in 1990; Amartya Sen received the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences in 1998.
